body.text: Midway through a recent candidates debate in a country shed, a rooster named Luke let out a panicked squawk and tried to break free.
The man holding Luke as a feathered political mascot was one of 12 candidates vying for the ultra-marginal seat of Ripon.
"Luke and I both believe in free speech, as he just demonstrated," said Bernard Quince, an independent who advocates the self-sufficiency benefits of owning a few chooks and a fruit tree.

For voters in this weekend's Victorian election, and perhaps all Australians, it was an unneeded reminder of how deeply unserious politics can appear, even in the face of its deeply serious consequences.
As Australians become "more pessimistic" and "more divided," trust in politicians has sagged to new lows, according to the Scanlon Foundation's social cohesion survey.
Candidates in the 14,444-square-kilometre electorate have been earnestly selling the idea they can be the change the public craves.
Not everyone's buying it.
"I don't think we can assume that our politicians have our best interests at heart," said Samantha Rickinson, a caravan park owner in Ararat, 200km out of Melbourne on the seat's western border.
Like so many segments of the country, exhaustion, distrust and outright anger are easily found.

Motorists have become adept at dodging potholes; ratepayers are locked in years-long battles with council for basic improvements; households are squeezed by cost-of-living pressures and infuriated by ballooning government debt.

"You could pick this electorate [of Ripon] up and plonk it into regional New South Wales or Queensland and get very similar responses from punters," said Kos Samaras from political polling firm Redbridge Group.
"They've lost trust in institutions, they've lost trust in their political system, they think that the established political order is not interested in fixing their problems."
In the picturesque town of Beaufort, local mechanic Chris Johnstone is a staunch advocate for his community, but he can gesture around at any number of issues that rile him up.
Trucks rumbling through the otherwise quiet main street are a reminder of an unbuilt and as-yet unfunded bypass.
A solar-powered bin a few metres away had, to his bewilderment, been installed in near-permanent shade.
For the president of the local business group, it amounts to a general sense that things are not working as they should, even if he's not sure what the answer is.
"It's taken a long time to make this mess,"
Mr Johnstone said.
"It'll take a lot longer to bring it back under control."
Pothole problem runs deep
No political ad or AI social media video will override the potholes on a voter's street.
Damaged and dangerous roads have long plagued regional communities, but durable solutions from politicians are harder to find.
"A politician likes to cut a ribbon on a new road, but you can't cut a ribbon on a repaired pothole," said Rob Pelletier, a horticulturist on the outskirts of Beaufort.
"It's now caught up with them after so many years of neglect."
In September, a motorcyclist died after reportedly hitting a pothole on a stretch of the much-maligned Western Highway, not far from Mr Pelletier's home.
The tragedy occurred in a state where roads are crumbling faster than the government can repair them.
Experts have bemoaned the "old techniques" used for maintenance. Former VicRoads staff have blamed privatisation.
Even those paid to fix them say the current system is failing local communities.
"I drive on these roads every day. I'm so pissed off about it too," said Greg*, a contractor in the area who didn't want to risk losing work by using his name.
Greg sees angry Facebook comments from his community, and understands why people are lashing out at politicians, or even contractors like him.
The pothole problem has loomed especially large over the election, with costly promises for change coming from all directions.
Greg is unconvinced any of the parties have a meaningful answer.
"The biggest cost of it is bureaucracy," he said.
"We'll spend an excessive amount of money fixing a small patch because they can't make their mind up about where the budget's going to go."
A pool with no water
The town of Maryborough is nestled in the north-east of Ripon, where temperatures can reach 45 degrees Celsius.
Locals like Rowena Butler are staring down a fifth summer without a public pool.
"We want it back," Ms Butler said.
The heritage-listed complex was closed in 2022 after an independent assessment found cracking and leaking in the 50-metre outdoor pool spelled its "end of life".
In the years since, millions in funding has been secured to demolish and rebuild it, with more committed during this election campaign.
"There are complexities, but there is no excuse," said Ms Butler.
"We don't have that sense of urgency, that sense of commitment together to get it done."
In the closing weeks of a fiercely contested campaign, the sitting Labor member in the seat of Ripon, Martha Haylett, issued a withering statement regarding the pool.
"We are sick to death of this council repeatedly coming and asking for further money," she wrote, while nonetheless committing to a further $5 million in funding "under very strict conditions".
Despite welcoming the commitment, which was matched by Liberal candidate Megan Read and The Nationals' Jo Armstrong, chief executive of the local council Peter Harriot pushed back on the criticism.
"There has been no mismanagement of this project," Mr Harriot from the Central Goldfields Shire Council recently told the ABC.
"If you are talking about the costs … look at some of the tunnels in Melbourne that go [over the budget]. We are nowhere in the league of those increases."
It's the sort of heated back-and-forth that can dehydrate the will of a community.
Ms Butler grew up spending summer nights at the pool and now has active children of her own, but said the experience had affected how she felt about all levels of politics.
"I [feel] estranged from power, that feeling of having influence, that feeling of hard work reaps reward,"
she said.
"I've done the hard work, I've volunteered, I've engaged with council — still there's no pool."
Burning anger
If voter enthusiasm can be gauged through the number of candidate posters around a town, there were few to be found in Ararat on the eve of the Ripon election.
A poster for independent Trevor Andrei, a self-described doomsday-prepper and "pureblood (unvaxxed)", was a rare exception, pinned up in the shopfront of a local takeaway.
A harried woman working solo in the shop shrugged when asked about it, saying she didn't know anything of the poster or the man on it.
Nearby at the caravan park, Samantha Rickinson has plenty of political opinions but no clear home for them just yet.

"I'm a swing voter, but I think more people need to pay attention to policies and not just to parties," said Ms Rickinson, who had four kids and had run the park with her husband for close to 10 years.
The business is feeling the brunt of cost-of-living pressures on holiday-makers, and haunted by the financial effects of the COVID-19 pandemic.
"Prior to COVID, I didn't pay much attention to state politics. Certainly do now," she said.
"For me, it was just that loss of control and almost realising that you don't matter to these people."
Liberal Jess Wilson is expected to be elected Victorian Premier on Saturday, marking a significant change in a state that has spent 12 years under Labor.
Ms Rickinson, who cites the state's debt as her biggest election concern and is anxious about the future of her business, has little faith any level of government can fix what she sees as broken.
"The state of our country is really frightening. Everyone is just hanging on and trying to survive, and it's just not a way to live," she said.
"I just don't feel like there's any trust at the moment."
That lack of trust and desire for something entirely different is what One Nation has seized on around the country.
Polls and betting markets suggest Donna Buxton, a speech pathologist from the north-west Victorian town of Charlton, is a slim favourite to win the seat of Ripon.
Ms Buxton was announced as the One Nation candidate alongside Pauline Hanson and Barnaby Joyce at a rowdy late August event in the farming town of Marnoo.
"We're sick of the current major political parties — that's Liberal as well as The Nationals," said Ben Duxson, a nearby farmer whose "Farmers Fightback" group helped organise the event.
"Everyone's looking for a change. We've got an alternative out there now."
Ms Hanson grinned as she hammered a fake nail through a coffin with the words "RIP Net Zero".
A wooden replica transmission tower with the words "Scrap VNI West", a locally-objected renewables-linked transmission line project, was set ablaze.
Hot flames against a dark country sky made for stark imagery, but Mr Duxson denied such stunts served to raise the political temperature.
"We're pretty passive out here," he said.
"To me, the left are the evil sort of side. They'll do anything."
'This actually isn't really normal'
On a Friday afternoon at the Ballarat Show, Liberal candidate, farmer and mum of four Megan Read hovered near the sandwich board signs of her One Nation opponent.
The sharp pop of balloons bursting at her stand at random intervals created a nervy tension.
"There has been safety issues and concerns raised in particular over the last month, and it is escalating. That is for all parties," said Ms Read, while meeting show-goers.
"It's always on the back of my mind."
Inside the neighbouring One Nation booth, Ms Buxton said she had encountered a type of community anger during the campaign that was "quite aggressive".
At a farmers' market the week earlier, an angry man hounded her and peppered her with abuse.
"It was just great that I had a whole heap of male volunteers to help, because I don't know what he would've been like had it just been myself," she said.
Over in the Devonshire Tea shed, Greens candidate Tim Drylie believed the influence of social media was having a "funhouse mirror effect", distorting local issues into culture wars.
"I've never experienced it quite like this," said Mr Drylie, a local shire councillor and former mayor.
"It's really corrosive for our local democracies."
Even as they jostle in the campaign's final straight, candidates have taken to sharing details with one another about members of the public who have made serious threats.
At the final candidate forum in Ararat, a wall of police stood outside the entrance to the local RSL.
Inside the venue, Labor's sitting member, Martha Haylett, said she'd had death threats during her four years in the job, some directed toward her baby son.
"The wake-up call with Helen Haines and how devastating that was, I think a lot of us politicians thought, 'Oh, hang on a minute, this actually isn't really normal,'" Ms Haylett said.

As independent Bernard Quince prepared a new chook for another political appearance, a small group outside loudly protested the removal of culturally significant trees as part of a nearby road project.
Attendees from the forum swore at them as they left the RSL.
The protesters responded in kind and the confrontation threatened to boil over into something violent.
At an earlier event for Nationals candidate Jo Armstrong, federal senator Bridget McKenzie wondered where all the anger was pushing Australian democracy.
"Do we retreat? Do we lock ourselves behind walls online? Do we bother telling everyone in Ararat we're coming to the pub and we're going to be here from 5pm till 6:30pm?" she said.
"I would hate to see the public square diminished because of that fear."
'The luckiest in the world'
There's an oasis-like quality to the luminescent turquoise carpet and stark white walls of the Ararat Mosque.
Workers from the local meatworks regularly stop by for prayer — so too travellers, some from nearby Halls Gap or passing through on their way to South Australia.
Earlier in the day, mosque caretaker Farouk Kassab had been tooling about at the men's shed with other retirees when the election was brought up.
"A lot of the men there said, 'Oh look, we hope whoever wins, it's not the ones aligned with the lady with the red hair.' And they weren't Muslim," said Mr Kassab.
"I just said I hope whoever wins will do a good job for the community."
Given the way Muslim Australians have been invoked during One Nation's ascension, he might have cause for a more hardened perspective on the election.
Having moved to Australia in 1969, Mr Kassab instead defaults to a more panoramic worldview, one informed by his experience living abroad.

"We have to be realistic — when we see the rest of the world, how tough it is, how bad it is, we can look at our situation and say, 'We thank God, that God has put us in this country,' which I believe is the best country in the world.
"The people that live here are the luckiest in the world. I appreciate it and enjoy it.
"I don't believe there is any country in the world that is better than Australia."
